## Why

The CSV export writes dates as the browser shows them, so the importer and the
spreadsheet read different days near midnight.

## Acceptance criteria

Each one is checked by something that can be run or looked at. No criterion without a check.

- [ ] A1: Every date in the export reads back as the same instant · check: `pnpm test`

- `src/csv/dates.ts`
- `src/csv/dates.test.ts`

## Out of scope

- No new dependencies.

## Questions for me

One question per line, in this shape; options are separated by `;`.

- [ ] (answer individually) Should the export write dates the way `toISOString()` does
      (`2026-11-25T10:00:00.000Z`, always UTC), or in the owner's zone, as the
      [RFC 3339 profile](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339#section-5.6) allows
      (`2026-11-25T11:00:00+01:00`)? The spreadsheet the owner opens it in reads both, but
      the importer at https://example.test/importer/v2 reads only the first, and
      `parseDate` in `src/csv/dates.ts` would need a second branch for the other, with its
      own tests for the hour either side of a clock change. —
      Recommended: UTC, as `toISOString()` writes it, with the zone named in the header
      row (`date (UTC)`). Options: the owner's zone, with its offset on every value; both,
      as two columns (`date (UTC)` and `date (local)`).
- [x] Quote every field, or only those that need it? — Recommended: only those that
      need it. Options: every field. — Owner: only those that need it.
- [ ] Name the file `report.csv` or `report-<date>.csv`? — Recommended:
      `report-<date>.csv`. Options: `report.csv`.
